newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts settle sharply lower on pound's slide.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts settle sharply lower on pound's slide.

text.p: UK gilts closed sharply lower on Wednesday on the back of rapidly sliding sterling, triggered by Bank of England Governor Eddie George's remarks that there was no urgent need for a dramatic interest rate rise.

"It has been a non-stop collapse today. The market's gone down much further and much faster than I thought it would," one salesman said. "Gilts have been underperforming virtually all other markets today."
The December gilt future settled at 110-13, down 27/32 on the day.
The gilt/Bund spread edged out to 190 basis points, which one trader referred to as "a very generous spread" and likely to lure in some overseas cash.
George took the market by surprise when he played down the need to steep rate rises.
"We don't see an urgent need for a dramatic step," he told the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee.
But when asked if this meant he expected no rate rise before the general election he said, "I certainly wouldn't go that far".
March short sterling jumped on George's remarks, settling at 93.38, up 10 basis points but off the session high of 93.46.
"Short sterling had a very strong bounce after George's comments on interest rates," one trader said. "It went from 93.28 to 93.46 in a matter of 15 minutes or so."
"People's perceptions of interest rates has changed. They're pushing their expectations of a rate rise back to February or March, rather than mid-December."
December short sterling settled up 0.06 at 93.61, still discounting a quarter point rate rise by the end of the year.
Most City economists expect George to call for higher interest rates when he meets Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke next week to discuss monetary policy.
But a Reuters poll conducted after the budget found a majority expected the cost of borrowing to stay on hold at 6.0 percent until the end of the year.
Dealers said the market could be in for another bumpy ride on Friday when domestic manufacturing data for October and the U.S. non-farm payroll data for November are due to be released.
The Reuter consensus foreast suggests UK manufacturing output rose 0.4 percent in the month and the U.S. payroll grew by 179,000.
"We're all going to be quite jittery, but we might just steady up ahead of non-farm payrolls," one dealer said.

"Of course, if it's a very low figure, the market should recover fast enough. Nobody's quite sure how far the collapse of currency will go, but we've probably seen the worst of the fall." -- Sonali Verma, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5978
